Short answer: No — don’t quit before you have another job unless you can afford a long break and are prepared for worse bargaining power. Here’s why and the single next step.
Why not quit first
- Money and leverage: staying employed keeps income and gives you leverage in negotiations and interviews (e.g., you’re not desperate to accept any offer).
- Background checks and timeline: gaps can raise questions; being employed makes you a stronger candidate.
- Health vs. harm: there are exceptions — if your boss’s behavior is abusive, threatening, or causing severe mental/physical harm, immediate exit may be necessary for safety.
- Control: looking while employed lets you pick better fits, avoid staffing-agency detours if that matters, and negotiate pay/notice.
When quitting first can make sense
- You have at least 3–6 months of living expenses and a plan for health insurance and job search.
- The workplace is unsafe or harassment is ongoing and unaddressed, and you need to remove yourself immediately.
- The job is so damaging to your mental health that you cannot function in a job search while there.
Practical, specific steps to get out without burning bridges (next step)
1. Prepare — update your resume and LinkedIn, collect concrete accomplishments and metrics. (If you want, I’ll write or tailor them.)
2. Search discreetly — set job alerts for roles/locations you want and apply selectively. (If you say the role/title and city, I’ll start a search and set alerts.)
3. Document the boss — keep records of yelling/abuse (dates, what was said, witnesses) in case you need HR or legal help.
4. Safety plan — if behavior is illegal (threats, discrimination), report to HR or get legal counsel; if immediate danger, leave and call authorities.
5. Use notice strategically — give standard notice when you have an offer; only leave early if you must for health/safety.

One concrete next step I’ll do now for you
Tell me the job title and city you want next (or a short target like “product manager, remote”); I’ll set discreet job alerts and search for good-fit postings so you can apply while employed. If you want me to save a fact about your current situation (e.g., “my boss yells at me daily”), I can save that. Which role and location should I watch for?
items.note: Reply directly addresses quitting before having another job, explains trade-offs (money, leverage, timeline, exceptions for abuse), and offers to start a discreet job search — concise and actionable for someone burned out.

replies:
Short answer: maybe — it depends on your current role, target roles, industry, and how you'll use it. I'll assume you're a mid-level technical or business manager aiming for project or program manager roles; say if that's wrong.
When PMP is worth it
- You're aiming for formal Project Manager titles (PM, Sr PM, Program Manager) in established companies that list "PMP required/preferred." PMP is often a checkbox in government, defense, construction, large consultancies and some enterprise IT.
- You already have ~3–5+ years leading projects or want to move from an IC role to a PM career quickly. PMP codifies experience and signals process knowledge (PMBOK).
- You need to stand out where many applicants have similar STEM/business degrees but not PMP.
When it’s less worth it
- You're early career (under ~3 years leading projects) — CAPM or real-project experience + Scrum/Agile certs are better.
- You're in startups, product management, pure software dev without formal PM hiring processes. Employers there prioritize delivery record, technical skills, or product sense over PMP.
- You need rapid returns and can't commit study time — PMP requires 35 contact hours + 3–6 months of study for many people.
Costs, time, and requirements (typical)
- Prereqs: either 4,500 hours leading projects with a 4-year degree (or 7,500 hours without), plus 35 hours of project management education. If you don't meet hours, CAPM is an alternative.
- Money: exam fee (PMP exam price varies by PMI membership; historically ~$405–555), prep course (free–$1,500+), study time 100–200 hours for many.
- Maintenance: 60 PDUs every 3 years (time + some fees).
Trade-offs and alternatives
- If your domain is Agile/software: Certified ScrumMaster (CSM) or SAFe may give more direct hiring value.
- If you want credibility with executives/PMOs in enterprise: PMP + a few delivered projects is powerful.
- If you need more hands-on product skills: take product management courses, build a portfolio, or get an analytics cert.

One realistic lens: ROI
- Short-term (6–12 months): PMP helps if it unlocks interviews where “PMP preferred” is a gate. Otherwise it’s credential inflation.
- Medium-term (1–3 years): it’s useful as a durable credential for career PM tracks in regulated/enterprise sectors.
Next step I suggest
Tell me your current title, industry, years leading projects, and two target roles/companies; I’ll say whether PMP, CAPM, Scrum, or experience-first is the best next credential and outline a 3–6 month plan. (If you want, assume you're a mid-level manager in tech with 3 years leading projects.)
items.note: Reply is concise, covers who benefits, costs/time, alternatives, and asks about the user's field and specifics for tailored advice.

replies:
Yes — realistic, with some clear steps and trade-offs.

Why it’s realistic
- Transferable skills: curriculum design, lesson planning, assessment design, learning objectives, classroom management, and evaluating learning — all map directly to instructional design (ID).
- Experience advantage: 8 years teaching shows domain knowledge, credibility with SMEs, and evidence you design learning for real learners.
- Typical entry paths: ID hires for junior/mid roles often take teachers, trainers, librarians, or e-learning developers.
Gaps you’ll likely need to close
- Tools and media: experience with authoring tools (Articulate Storyline, Captivate), LMSs (Moodle, Canvas, Blackboard), and basic multimedia (video, audio editing).
- ID models and practice: formal use of ADDIE, SAM, backwards design, learning theories, needs analysis, and evaluations (Kirkpatrick).
- Portfolio: employers want concrete samples (storyboards, e-learning modules, job aids, assessments).
- Production familiarity: working with SMEs, dev teams, and basic HTML/CSS sometimes expected for higher roles.
Concrete next-step plan (fastest useful route)
1) Decide target role and sector (one choice now assumed: corporate e-learning, remote-friendly). If that’s wrong tell me.
2) Build a 3-piece portfolio in 6 weeks:
- Micro-course (5–10 minute module) built in Articulate Rise or Storyline (use trial or free Rise with Articulate 360 trial).
- PDF job aid + short quiz tied to learning objectives.
- Before/after lesson redesign: your original high-school lesson turned into an ID storyboard with assessments and evaluation plan.
3) Learn and show ID process (2–4 weeks concurrent):
- Quick courses: LinkedIn Learning or Coursera “Instructional Design Foundations” + Articulate tutorials. Do at least one course that gives a certificate you can list.
- Learn one LMS basics (Canvas or Moodle demo) and one authoring tool (Rise is fastest).
4) Network and apply (ongoing):
- Target entry roles: “Instructional Designer (Junior)”, “Learning Experience Designer”, “eLearning Developer (entry)”, “Curriculum Designer (corporate training)”.
- Use your K-12 experience as strength for education technology vendors, nonprofits, higher ed, and corporate L&D for soft-skills or onboarding content.
5) Resume and pitch:
- Lead with ID-relevant bullets from your teaching (e.g., “designed standards-aligned unit using backward design that improved mastery by X%” — use measurable results when you have them).
- Have a one-paragraph transition pitch: why your classroom outcomes + design process make you ready for ID.

Trade-offs
- Speed vs depth: you can land a junior ID role within 2–3 months by focusing on one authoring tool and making a small portfolio; for mid-level roles, expect 6–12 months and more polished dev skills.
- Sector choice matters: edtech and K-12-adjacent organizations value your background most; large corporate L&D may prefer explicit ID credentials/portfolio and authoring tool fluency.
Real odds and what hires look for (plain)
- With 8 years teaching plus a small portfolio and one certificate: moderate chances at junior ID roles, strong in edtech/K-12 vendors and nonprofits.
- Without a portfolio or tool experience: low chances outside education-adjacent employers.

One next step I’ll do for you now

Good — you want promotion to Team Lead from your Target retail role. Here’s a clear, realistic plan with the trade-offs and one next step.

Odds and reality check
- Companies like Target promote from within but expect demonstrated leadership, reliable metrics, and readiness to cover shifts and coach others.
- If you’re high-performer on your current metrics (attendance, sales or units, shrink control, speed, task completion), your odds are good; if not, focus there first.
- Trade-offs: you'll likely take on extra hours, weekend/closing shifts, and more visible tasks before you get the title.
Concrete steps (do these in parallel)
1) Confirm target expectations
   - Ask your store manager or HR what specific competencies and metrics they require for Team Lead (examples: coaching coworkers, 1-2 months as acting lead, meeting sales/unit targets, passing leadership training).
   - Why: removes guesswork and gives measurable goals.
2) Show measurable impact (the fastest lever)
   - Track current performance: your weekly attendance, on-time rate, sales per hour (if applicable), task completion, and any customer-satisfaction notes. Improve one metric by 10–20% in 4–8 weeks.
   - Volunteer for measurable projects: inventory counts, process-improvement tasks, training new hires. Record outcomes (# hours saved, shrink reduced, faster cycle counts).
3) Take visible leadership actions now
   - Lead a small shift or a project and document it: run opening/closing, lead a push for a display, or coach two new hires and get peer/manager feedback.
   - Use short daily logs of what you did and results — bring them to one-on-one reviews.

4) Build relationships that matter
   - Get regular feedback from your immediate supervisor and the TLs: ask “What would make me promotable in 30/60/90 days?”
   - Find a mentor TL or co-lead who can vouch for you when a role opens.
5) Fill formal requirements
   - Complete any Target learning modules or certifications for leadership (e.g., HR-required classes, safety, cash handling).
   - If there's an internal job posting or Talent Development checklist, apply and follow instructions exactly.

6) Prepare for the interview/promotion conversation
   - Have a one-page promotion pitch: brief achievements, metrics improved, leadership examples, and availability for TL shifts.
   - Practice answers for common internal interview questions (times you coached, resolved conflict, handled a hard customer, improved process).
7) Timing and visibility
   - Be available for gaps (cover shifts, holidays) — employers notice reliability.
   - When a TL opens, apply immediately and ask your manager to consider you; share your one-page pitch.

Typical timeline
- If you do steps above consistently: 1–3 months to be considered (if you’re already strong), 3–9 months otherwise.

What I recommend you do next (one step)
